text: The land here emptied partly because of a war the Potawatomi never fought.
It started with lead.
After miners struck ore around Galena in the 1820s,
they poured onto ground the Sauk and Meskwaki still farmed and shoved them west of the Mississippi.
Black Hawk would not stay shoved.
In the spring of 1832, the sixty-five-year-old Sauk leader led about a thousand Sauk, Meskwaki,
and Kickapoo back across the river, most of them women and children,
to plant corn on land a disputed 1804 treaty had signed away.
Black Hawk and others called that treaty worthless.
The men who signed it, he said, never had the right to sell.
Illinois settlers raised a militia anyway.
The Black Hawk War ran from April to August.
It ended on the second of August at the mouth of the Bad Axe River in Wisconsin,
where soldiers and militia opened fire on people waving a white flag, trying to surrender.
A thousand had crossed in spring.
Roughly a hundred and fifty lived to see the fall.
The war was short, and the government read its lesson plainly.
Native nations that stayed could be removed, and the Northwest thrown open to settlers.
The Indian Removal Act of 1830 had already written that into law.
Now the army had proven it could be done.
